<comment datatype="string">The growth of <i>E. coli</i> on short-chain fatty acids (C3-C6) requires the activation of the acids to their respective
thioesters.  This activation is catalyzed by acetoacetyl-CoA transferase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1103739">Sramek75</a>].  The reaction takes place
in two half-reactions which involves a covalent enzyme-CoA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1103741">Sramek75a</a>].  The enzyme undergoes two
detectable conformational changes during the reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/332081">Sramek77</a>].  It is thought likely that the reaction
proceeds by a ping-pong mechanism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1103741">Sramek75a</a>].  The enzyme can utilize a variety of short-chain acyl-CoA
and carboxylic acid substrates but exhibits maximal activity with normal and 3-keto substrates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1103739">Sramek75</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers
with a low reduction potential.
In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in
the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes
and the storage of iron and sulfur.
In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate
in gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637">Park06</a>].
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers
with a low reduction potential.
In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in
the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes
and the storage of iron and sulfur.
In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate
in gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637">Park06</a>].
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways.
Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers
with a low reduction potential.
In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in
the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes
and the storage of iron and sulfur.
In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate
in gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637">Park06</a>].
<p>
[4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure.  The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. 
<p>
Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3.
<p>
In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates and are thus classified as enzyme cofactors. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.8.1.8">EC 2.8.1.8, lipoyl synthase</a>, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29051382">McCarthy17</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways.
Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers
with a low reduction potential.
In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in
the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes
and the storage of iron and sulfur.
In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate
in gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637">Park06</a>].
<p>
[4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure.  The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. 
<p>
Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3.
<p>
In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates and are thus classified as enzyme cofactors. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.8.1.8">EC 2.8.1.8, lipoyl synthase</a>, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29051382">McCarthy17</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">The soluble NADH dehydrogenase fragment consisting of the NuoE, NuoF and NuoG subunits represents the electron input part of NADH dehydrogenase I [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7607227">Leif95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9485311">Braun98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10544236">Bungert99</a>].

<comment datatype="string">Iron-sulfur clusters are cofators of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=FeS-Proteins">iron-sulfur proteins</a> and consist of a cluster of two to four iron atoms linked to sulfides, some of which are cysteine residues of the protein.
<p>
Several cluster types have been described, including <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>Iron-sulfur clusters</a> consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression regulation [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;In <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains.">a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-23" title="Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers&#10;with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur.&#10;In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;">a [3Fe-3S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=3FE-4S" title="Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers&#10;with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur.&#10;In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;">a [3Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-7" title="Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways.&#10;Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers&#10;with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur.&#10;In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;[4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure.  The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. &#10;&#10;Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3.&#10;&#10;In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates and are thus classified as enzyme cofactors. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.8.1.8''>EC 2.8.1.8, lipoyl synthase</a>, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29051382''>McCarthy17</a>].">a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is relatively rare, and 3Fe/4Fe interconversion may occur with minimal protein reorganization. In another type of Fe-S cluster, known as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD0-1098" title="Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;Rieske iron-sulfur clusters contain two iron atoms and two sulfur atoms, similar to an <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. However, while in <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains, in Rieske clusters a pair of cysteinyl residues on one of the iron centers are replaced by 2 imidazole ligands from the side chain of two histidine residues.">a Rieske [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, two of the 4 cysteine residues that are coordinated with the iron atoms in regular <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>Iron-sulfur clusters</a> consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression regulation [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;In <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains.">a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> are substituted by histidine residues. Although the clusters contain several iron atoms, each one usually transfers only one electron, so, for example, a protein with two [4Fe-4S] clusters will usually transfer two electrons.
<p>
Small electron transfer proteins that contain only [2Fe-2S] or [4Fe-4S] clusters are called <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Ferredoxins">ferredoxins</a>. When Fe-S clusters occur in larger (and sometimes membrane-bound) proteins together with other prosthetic groups and/or metal cofactors, the proteins are designated as complex Fe-S proteins. 
<p>
In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in
the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes
and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637">Park06</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Iron-sulfur clusters are cofators of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=FeS-Proteins">iron-sulfur proteins</a> and consist of a cluster of two to four iron atoms linked to sulfides, some of which are cysteine residues of the protein.
<p>
Several cluster types have been described, including <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>Iron-sulfur clusters</a> consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression regulation [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;In <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains.">a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-23" title="Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers&#10;with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur.&#10;In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;">a [3Fe-3S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=3FE-4S" title="Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers&#10;with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur.&#10;In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;">a [3Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> and <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-7" title="Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways.&#10;Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers&#10;with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in&#10;the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes&#10;and the storage of iron and sulfur.&#10;In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;[4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters feature four iron ions and four sulfide ions placed at the vertices of a cubane-type structure.  The Fe centers are typically further coordinated by cysteinyl ligands. &#10;&#10;Two main types of [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters are low-potential (bacterial-type) clusters and high-potential (HiPIP) clusters. The bacterial clusters shift between the oxidation states +1 and +2, while the HiPIP clusters shift between the oxidation states +2 and +3.&#10;&#10;In some enzymes the [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur clusters bind substrates and are thus classified as enzyme cofactors. For example, in radical SAM enzymes the cluster binds and reduces S-adenosylmethionine, generating a radical that interacts with the enzyme's substrate. In a few cases, as in <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=EC-NUMBER&object=EC-2.8.1.8''>EC 2.8.1.8, lipoyl synthase</a>, the cluster serves as the source of sulfur atoms for a sulfuration reaction [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29051382''>McCarthy17</a>].">a [4Fe-4S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. The [3Fe-4S] cluster is relatively rare, and 3Fe/4Fe interconversion may occur with minimal protein reorganization. In another type of Fe-S cluster, known as <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD0-1098" title="Iron-sulfur centers consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. Iron-sulfur clusters are prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate&#10;in gene expression [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;Rieske iron-sulfur clusters contain two iron atoms and two sulfur atoms, similar to an <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>. However, while in <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains, in Rieske clusters a pair of cysteinyl residues on one of the iron centers are replaced by 2 imidazole ligands from the side chain of two histidine residues.">a Rieske [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a>, two of the 4 cysteine residues that are coordinated with the iron atoms in regular <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6" title="<a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=FeS-Centers''>Iron-sulfur clusters</a> consist of nonheme iron complexed to sulfur in several ways. They serve as prosthetic groups of many proteins, which function as intracellular electron carriers with a low reduction potential.&#10;In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes and the storage of iron and sulfur. They act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression regulation [<a href=''http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637''>Park06</a>].&#10;&#10;In <a href=''/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=CPD-6''>a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> the irons are coordinated to the sulfurs of 4 cysteine side chains.">a [2Fe-2S] iron-sulfur cluster</a> are substituted by histidine residues. Although the clusters contain several iron atoms, each one usually transfers only one electron, so, for example, a protein with two [4Fe-4S] clusters will usually transfer two electrons.
<p>
Small electron transfer proteins that contain only [2Fe-2S] or [4Fe-4S] clusters are called <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=Ferredoxins">ferredoxins</a>. When Fe-S clusters occur in larger (and sometimes membrane-bound) proteins together with other prosthetic groups and/or metal cofactors, the proteins are designated as complex Fe-S proteins. 
<p>
In addition to their roles in electron transfer reactions, iron-sulfur clusters are also known to participate in
the activation of substrates, the stabilization of radicals and structures, the protection of proteins from enzymes
and the storage of iron and sulfur. In addition, they act as sensors of iron, dioxygen, the superoxide ion, and possibly nitric oxide, and participate in gene expression [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16466637">Park06</a>].</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Menaquinols are the reduced form of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Menaquinones" title="Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. <comment datatype="string">Menaquinols are the reduced form of <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Menaquinones" title="Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. <p>

<comment datatype="string">Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are isoprenoid quinones of the naphthalene series, and are constituents of bacterial plasma membranes, where they play important roles in electron transfer and oxidative phosphorylation. Menaquinones are the most widespread respiratory quinones in biological systems [<a href="http://cdn.intechopen.com/pdfs/28774/InTech-Menaquinone_as_well_as_ubiquinone_as_a_crucial_component_in_the_escherichia_coli_respiratory_chain.pdf">Fujimoto12</a>]. Menaquinones and demethylmenaquinones are named MK-<i>n</i> or DMK-<i>n</i>, respectively, where the <i>n</i> refers to the number of prenyl units present in the side chain. The most common length of the side chain in bacteria is 8, although minor amounts of MK-1 through MK-14 have been found [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7022156">Collins81</a>].
<p>
Many bacteria and archaea have <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?type=COMPOUND&object=Dihydromenaquinones">dehydrogenated menaquinones</a>, which are named MK-<i>n</i>(H<sub>2</sub>). The degree and location of dehydrogenation depends on the species. Some organisms have menaquinones with modifications of the head group, for example <a href="/META/NEW-IMAGE?object=TAX-2302"><i>Thermoplasma</i></a> possess both <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-15875">thermoplasmaquinones</a> (TPQ), which contains an extra methyl group, and <a href="/compound?orgid=META&id=CPD-15876">methionaquinones</a> (MTK), which contains a methylthio group [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11157962">Shimada01</a>].
<p>
Menaquinones are also known as vitamin K<sub>2</sub>. Vitamin K is a name given to a group of derivatives  of 2-methyl-1,4-naphthoquinone that are required by mammals for the posttranslational modification of certain proteins, mostly involved in blood coagulation. These compounds, while essential for mammals, are not synthesized by them, and are thus considered vitamins.
<p>

<comment datatype="string">NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase I (NDH-1) is an NADH dehydrogenase that catalyzes the transfer of electrons from NADH to the quinone pool in the cytoplasmic membrane and is able to generate a proton electrochemical gradient. It is part of both the aerobic and anaerobic respiratory chain of the cell. The study of this enzyme is of great interest, because it is considered to be a structurally minimal form of a proton-pumping NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase and serves as a model for the more complex mitochondrial enzyme.
<p>
NDH-1 is one of two distinct NADH dehydrogenases in <i>E. coli</i>. In contrast to <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=NADH-DHII-MONOMER">NDH-2</a> (encoded by <i>ndh</i>), NDH-1-catalyzed electron flow from NADH to ubiquinone generates an electrochemical gradient. Depending on the strain, NDH-2 utilizes NADH exclusively, while NDH-1 can utilize both NADH and d-NADH, which enables specific assays of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3122832">Matsushita87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2679883">Hayashi89</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8387992">Calhoun93</a>].
<p>
NDH-1 appears to exist in a resting and an active form [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27148945">Belevich16</a>]. A conformational change upon activation was mapped to the junction of the hydrophilic and membrane domains. A tightly bound ubiquinone is reduced in the resting form, and a loosely bound ubiquinol can be exchanged with pool quinones in the active form [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28070565">Belevich17</a>]. Activation of NDH-1 appears to depend on conversion from a state where NADH dehydrogenation is decoupled from proton pumping to a coupled state where proton pumping occurs [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28960069">Belevich17a</a>]. The mechanism that couples electron transfer with proton pumping involves a catalytically important quinol anion [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34026733">Nuber21</a>].
<p>
The FMN binding constant is significantly lower for the oxidized NDH-1 (femto- to picomolar) than for the NADH-reduced enzyme (nanomolar). FMN's ability to reversibly dissociate from the enzyme is linked to the relatively high redox potential of the off-pathway N1a iron-sulfur cluster [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27555334">Holt16</a>]. The presence of the N1a cluster appears to be required for stability of NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28509551">Dorner17</a>]. Reduction of N1a increases the binding affinity for NAD<sup>+</sup> and reduces the production of reactive oxygen species [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28821859">Gnandt17</a>]. Mechanistically, the reduction state of N1a determines the orientation of a peptide bond that is involved in the release of NAD<sup>+</sup>; it therefore appears to function as a molecular switch that regulates NADH oxidation in response to the redox state of NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31186428">Schulte19</a>].  
<p>
Crystal structures of the membrane domain of NDH-1 have been solved at 3.9 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20505720">Efremov10</a>] and later at 3 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21822288">Efremov11</a>]. The striking placement within the NDH-1 complex of NuoL's long amphipathic &alpha;-helix suggested that proton translocation may be facilitated by a piston-like movement of this helix [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20505720">Efremov10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20505714">Ohnishi10</a>]. However, analysis of an extensive set of NuoL mutants and analysis of movement of the amphipathic helix of NuoL indicate that it does not function as a mechanical piston and may instead function like a clamp for the NuoLMN subunits during catalytic turnover [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22060017">Belevich11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26115017">Steimle15</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26134569">Zhu15</a>]. The exact number of protons translocated across the membrane remains unknown; the H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> stoichiometry is at least 1.5 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8892824">Bogachev96</a>]. Recent experiments argue for at least two coupling sites for proton translocation, with NuoL being essential for the translocation of 2H<sup>+</sup>/2e<sup>-</sup> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21417432">Steimle11</a>]. A crystal structure of the membrane component at higher resolution has allowed identification of possible proton translocation pathways and argues for a purely conformation-driven pathway of proton translocation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21822288">Efremov11</a>]. Zn<sup>2+</sup> inhibits Ndh-1, possibly by blocking the entry or exit of a proton translocation pathway [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25238255">Schulte14</a>].
<p>
Based on a stoichiometry of 4 H<sup>+</sup> translocated per NADH oxidized (2e<sup>-</sup>), a mixed model for proton translocation using both direct (redox-driven) and indirect (conformation-driven) mechanisms for proton pumping has been presented [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21454533">Treberg11</a>]. However, a lower ratio of 3H<sup>+</sup>/2e<sup>-</sup> has recently been proposed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22392981">Wikstrom12</a>]. Mg<sup>2+</sup> appears to be required for the proton pumping activity of NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27118783">Narayanan16</a>]. The Ndh-1 catalytic cycle has been followed in real time, revealing an essentially biphasic reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25283488">Belevich14</a>].
<p>
The purified enzyme can be separated into three components: a soluble fragment composed of the NuoE, F and G subunits which catalyzes the oxidation of NADH, representing the electron input part of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9485311">Braun98</a>]; an amphipathic connecting fragment composed of the NuoB, CD and I subunits; and a hydrophobic membrane fragment composed of the NuoA, H, J, K, L, M and N subunits [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7607227">Leif95</a>]. The soluble subunits contain all iron-sulfur clusters and the FMN cofactor; the redox properties of those cofactors have been studied [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18269245">Euro08</a>], and their intrinsic redox potential was modeled [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20513348">Medvedev10</a>]. Electron transfer from NADH via FMN to the iron-sulfur centers has been measured in real time by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18316732">Verkhovskaya08</a>] and later by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25600069">deVries15</a>], showing different results potentially due to methodological differences. Results from crosslinking analysis suggest that the ubiquinone-binding site of the enzyme is located on the membrane subunit NuoM [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12730198">Gong03b</a>], but it has also been modeled to the interface between NuoB and NuoCD based on its location in the <i>T. thermophilus</i> enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17157874">Baranova07a</a>]. Site-directed spin labeling is being used for localization of the ubiquinone binding site [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20959113">Pohl10</a>]. There may be two ubiquinone binding sites [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22580197">Verkhovsky12</a>], and NDH-1 purified using a new procedure contained two molecules of ubiquinone per complex [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23543743">Narayanan13</a>]. A tightly bound ubiquinone found by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24216024">Verkhovskaya14</a>] has a very low midpoint potential of < -300 mV, while two quinone radicals found by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24279322">Hielscher13</a>] had midpoint potentials of -37 and -235 mV. EPR signals from three semiquinone intermediates have been detected, and their properties were characterized [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25868873">Narayanan15</a>].
<p>
The NuoJ [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15736965">Kao05b</a>], NuoK [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14730982">Kervinen04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15996109">Kao05a</a>], NuoM [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17977822">TorresBacete07</a>] and NuoN [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12718520">Amarneh03</a>] subunits are implicated in the ability to generate an electrochemical gradient.  Molecular dynamics simulations of the membrane domain have established a possible coupling mechanism for energy transduction within NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24778264">Kaila14</a>].
<p>
Three-dimensional reconstruction and 2-D crystals of the NDH-1 complex based on cryo-electron microscopy showed an L-shaped form with an integral membrane and a peripheral arm [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9514725">Guenebaut98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12923180">Holt03</a>]. A model of the spatial arrangement of the subunits and the possible functional mechanism of proton pumping has been proposed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12923180">Holt03</a>]. Under low ionic strength conditions, the complex appears to adopt a horseshoe-like conformation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11880370">Bottcher02</a>]. Cryo-electron microscopy of the membrane domain allowed calculation of a projection structure at 8 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17157874">Baranova07a</a>]; later, a cryo-EM 3D structure of the intact NDH-1 complex was obtained [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18433710">Morgan08</a>]. Binding of NADH induces a conformational change in both the membrane and peripheral arm of NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15037611">Mamedova04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18793172">Pohl08</a>]. A mechanism by which the redox reaction of the N2 Fe-S cluster induces a conformational change that may lead to proton translocation has been proposed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20214873">Friedrich</a>]. A single-particle cryo-EM structure of the entire NDH-1 complex suggested a new coupling mechanism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34308841">Kolata21</a>]
<p>
Heterooligomers of NDH-1 and NDH-2 have been identified by electrophoresis and sucrose gradient centrifugation suggestive of a supramolecular organisation in the membrane [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21040753">Sousa11</a>].
<p>
NDH-1 is required for the anaerobic respiration of NADH using fumarate or DMSO as the terminal electron acceptors, thus implying that the enzyme can transfer electrons to menaquinone [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9063459">Tran97</a>]. The comparative energy efficiency of utilization of the various components of the aerobic respiratory chain has been examined [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8491720">Calhoun93a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>].  
<p>
Stolpe and Friedrich [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14970214">Stolpe04</a>] showed that NDH-1 is primarily an electrogenic proton pump which may have secondary Na<sup>+</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> antiport activity. However, contrary to the generally accepted view, Steuber et al. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10652103">Steuber00</a>] suggested that NDH-1 functions primarily as a Na<sup>+</sup> pump, a function that can be conveyed by a truncated form of the NuoL subunit alone [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12740360">Steuber03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17583799">Gemperli07</a>].   
<p>
NDH-1 produces reactive oxygen species, mainly in the form of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, at the NADH dehydrogenase active site, involving the FMN cofactor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18307315">Esterhazy08</a>]. NADH-dependent production of hydrogen peroxide is increased in a NuoF E95Q mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24325249">Knuuti13</a>]. The rate of O<sub>2</sub> reduction is dependent on the NAD<sup>+</sup>/NADH ratio [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18307315">Esterhazy08</a>]. 
<p>
Purified NDH-1 is activated by detergent and phospholipids [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15938640">Sinegina05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14970214">Stolpe04</a>]. A tightly bound metal, most likely Ca<sup>2+</sup>, is required for activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20840839">Verkhovskaya11</a>] and stability [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29668960">Belevich18</a>]. Proteins involved in the assembly and stability of NDH-1 have been identified [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30251413">Burschel19</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32777304">Oppermann20</a>]. Exposure to tellurite damages NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25447814">DiazVasquez15</a>].
<p>
Mutants lacking NDH-1 can not compete with wild type in stationary phase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8366049">Zambrano93</a>]. Expression of the <i>nuo</i> operon is regulated by oxygen, nitrate, fumarate, and other factors including C4 dicarboxylates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7565112">Bongaerts95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9063459">Tran97</a>]. Transcription and activity of aerobic respiratory chain components in the different phases of aerobic growth have been measured [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22700653">Sousa12</a>].
<p>
A phylogenomics analysis of NDH-1 subunits suggested that an ancestral NDH-1 complex may have already been present in the Last Universal Cellular Ancestor (LUCA) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27449624">Novakovsky16</a>].
<p>
Mutations in NDH-1 components, predominantly in the membrane arm of the complex, were identified in a laboratory evolution experiment selecting for increased persister cell formation upon entry into stationary phase. The mutations generally impair the proton translocation activity of NDH-1; the resulting cytoplasmic acidification appears to be the cause for increased persister cell formation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35087069">Van22</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26944855">Gnandt16</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26807915">Berrisford16</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26682761">Friedrich16</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24973951">Sato14</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25077450">NakamaruOgiso14</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24059518">Sazanov13</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23701194">Kanjee13</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20505714">Ohnishi10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18394423">Schneider08a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17274631">Sazanov07</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14741580">Friedrich04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12600193">Yagi03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11695826">Friedrich01a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10940377">Friedrich00a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9593887">Ohnishi98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9593861">Friedrich98a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7984099">Neijssel94</a>, <a href="http://www.ecosal.org/">EcoSal</a>]

<comment datatype="string">NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase I (NDH-1) is an NADH dehydrogenase that catalyzes the transfer of electrons from NADH to the quinone pool in the cytoplasmic membrane and is able to generate a proton electrochemical gradient. It is part of both the aerobic and anaerobic respiratory chain of the cell. The study of this enzyme is of great interest, because it is considered to be a structurally minimal form of a proton-pumping NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase and serves as a model for the more complex mitochondrial enzyme.
<p>
NDH-1 is one of two distinct NADH dehydrogenases in <i>E. coli</i>. In contrast to <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=NADH-DHII-MONOMER">NDH-2</a> (encoded by <i>ndh</i>), NDH-1-catalyzed electron flow from NADH to ubiquinone generates an electrochemical gradient. Depending on the strain, NDH-2 utilizes NADH exclusively, while NDH-1 can utilize both NADH and d-NADH, which enables specific assays of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3122832">Matsushita87</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2679883">Hayashi89</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8387992">Calhoun93</a>].
<p>
NDH-1 appears to exist in a resting and an active form [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27148945">Belevich16</a>]. A conformational change upon activation was mapped to the junction of the hydrophilic and membrane domains. A tightly bound ubiquinone is reduced in the resting form, and a loosely bound ubiquinol can be exchanged with pool quinones in the active form [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28070565">Belevich17</a>]. Activation of NDH-1 appears to depend on conversion from a state where NADH dehydrogenation is decoupled from proton pumping to a coupled state where proton pumping occurs [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28960069">Belevich17a</a>]. The mechanism that couples electron transfer with proton pumping involves a catalytically important quinol anion [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34026733">Nuber21</a>].
<p>
The FMN binding constant is significantly lower for the oxidized NDH-1 (femto- to picomolar) than for the NADH-reduced enzyme (nanomolar). FMN's ability to reversibly dissociate from the enzyme is linked to the relatively high redox potential of the off-pathway N1a iron-sulfur cluster [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27555334">Holt16</a>]. The presence of the N1a cluster appears to be required for stability of NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28509551">Dorner17</a>]. Reduction of N1a increases the binding affinity for NAD<sup>+</sup> and reduces the production of reactive oxygen species [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28821859">Gnandt17</a>]. Mechanistically, the reduction state of N1a determines the orientation of a peptide bond that is involved in the release of NAD<sup>+</sup>; it therefore appears to function as a molecular switch that regulates NADH oxidation in response to the redox state of NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31186428">Schulte19</a>].  
<p>
Crystal structures of the membrane domain of NDH-1 have been solved at 3.9 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20505720">Efremov10</a>] and later at 3 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21822288">Efremov11</a>]. The striking placement within the NDH-1 complex of NuoL's long amphipathic &alpha;-helix suggested that proton translocation may be facilitated by a piston-like movement of this helix [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20505720">Efremov10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20505714">Ohnishi10</a>]. However, analysis of an extensive set of NuoL mutants and analysis of movement of the amphipathic helix of NuoL indicate that it does not function as a mechanical piston and may instead function like a clamp for the NuoLMN subunits during catalytic turnover [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22060017">Belevich11</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26115017">Steimle15</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26134569">Zhu15</a>]. The exact number of protons translocated across the membrane remains unknown; the H<sup>+</sup>/e<sup>-</sup> stoichiometry is at least 1.5 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8892824">Bogachev96</a>]. Recent experiments argue for at least two coupling sites for proton translocation, with NuoL being essential for the translocation of 2H<sup>+</sup>/2e<sup>-</sup> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21417432">Steimle11</a>]. A crystal structure of the membrane component at higher resolution has allowed identification of possible proton translocation pathways and argues for a purely conformation-driven pathway of proton translocation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21822288">Efremov11</a>]. Zn<sup>2+</sup> inhibits Ndh-1, possibly by blocking the entry or exit of a proton translocation pathway [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25238255">Schulte14</a>].
<p>
Based on a stoichiometry of 4 H<sup>+</sup> translocated per NADH oxidized (2e<sup>-</sup>), a mixed model for proton translocation using both direct (redox-driven) and indirect (conformation-driven) mechanisms for proton pumping has been presented [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21454533">Treberg11</a>]. However, a lower ratio of 3H<sup>+</sup>/2e<sup>-</sup> has recently been proposed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22392981">Wikstrom12</a>]. Mg<sup>2+</sup> appears to be required for the proton pumping activity of NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27118783">Narayanan16</a>]. The Ndh-1 catalytic cycle has been followed in real time, revealing an essentially biphasic reaction [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25283488">Belevich14</a>].
<p>
The purified enzyme can be separated into three components: a soluble fragment composed of the NuoE, F and G subunits which catalyzes the oxidation of NADH, representing the electron input part of the enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9485311">Braun98</a>]; an amphipathic connecting fragment composed of the NuoB, CD and I subunits; and a hydrophobic membrane fragment composed of the NuoA, H, J, K, L, M and N subunits [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7607227">Leif95</a>]. The soluble subunits contain all iron-sulfur clusters and the FMN cofactor; the redox properties of those cofactors have been studied [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18269245">Euro08</a>], and their intrinsic redox potential was modeled [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20513348">Medvedev10</a>]. Electron transfer from NADH via FMN to the iron-sulfur centers has been measured in real time by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18316732">Verkhovskaya08</a>] and later by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25600069">deVries15</a>], showing different results potentially due to methodological differences. Results from crosslinking analysis suggest that the ubiquinone-binding site of the enzyme is located on the membrane subunit NuoM [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12730198">Gong03b</a>], but it has also been modeled to the interface between NuoB and NuoCD based on its location in the <i>T. thermophilus</i> enzyme [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17157874">Baranova07a</a>]. Site-directed spin labeling is being used for localization of the ubiquinone binding site [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20959113">Pohl10</a>]. There may be two ubiquinone binding sites [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22580197">Verkhovsky12</a>], and NDH-1 purified using a new procedure contained two molecules of ubiquinone per complex [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23543743">Narayanan13</a>]. A tightly bound ubiquinone found by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24216024">Verkhovskaya14</a>] has a very low midpoint potential of < -300 mV, while two quinone radicals found by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24279322">Hielscher13</a>] had midpoint potentials of -37 and -235 mV. EPR signals from three semiquinone intermediates have been detected, and their properties were characterized [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25868873">Narayanan15</a>].
<p>
The NuoJ [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15736965">Kao05b</a>], NuoK [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14730982">Kervinen04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15996109">Kao05a</a>], NuoM [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17977822">TorresBacete07</a>] and NuoN [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12718520">Amarneh03</a>] subunits are implicated in the ability to generate an electrochemical gradient.  Molecular dynamics simulations of the membrane domain have established a possible coupling mechanism for energy transduction within NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24778264">Kaila14</a>].
<p>
Three-dimensional reconstruction and 2-D crystals of the NDH-1 complex based on cryo-electron microscopy showed an L-shaped form with an integral membrane and a peripheral arm [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9514725">Guenebaut98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12923180">Holt03</a>]. A model of the spatial arrangement of the subunits and the possible functional mechanism of proton pumping has been proposed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12923180">Holt03</a>]. Under low ionic strength conditions, the complex appears to adopt a horseshoe-like conformation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11880370">Bottcher02</a>]. Cryo-electron microscopy of the membrane domain allowed calculation of a projection structure at 8 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17157874">Baranova07a</a>]; later, a cryo-EM 3D structure of the intact NDH-1 complex was obtained [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18433710">Morgan08</a>]. Binding of NADH induces a conformational change in both the membrane and peripheral arm of NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15037611">Mamedova04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18793172">Pohl08</a>]. A mechanism by which the redox reaction of the N2 Fe-S cluster induces a conformational change that may lead to proton translocation has been proposed [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20214873">Friedrich</a>]. A single-particle cryo-EM structure of the entire NDH-1 complex suggested a new coupling mechanism [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/34308841">Kolata21</a>]
<p>
Heterooligomers of NDH-1 and NDH-2 have been identified by electrophoresis and sucrose gradient centrifugation suggestive of a supramolecular organisation in the membrane [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21040753">Sousa11</a>].
<p>
NDH-1 is required for the anaerobic respiration of NADH using fumarate or DMSO as the terminal electron acceptors, thus implying that the enzyme can transfer electrons to menaquinone [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9063459">Tran97</a>]. The comparative energy efficiency of utilization of the various components of the aerobic respiratory chain has been examined [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8491720">Calhoun93a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>].  
<p>
Stolpe and Friedrich [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14970214">Stolpe04</a>] showed that NDH-1 is primarily an electrogenic proton pump which may have secondary Na<sup>+</sup>/H<sup>+</sup> antiport activity. However, contrary to the generally accepted view, Steuber et al. [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10652103">Steuber00</a>] suggested that NDH-1 functions primarily as a Na<sup>+</sup> pump, a function that can be conveyed by a truncated form of the NuoL subunit alone [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12740360">Steuber03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17583799">Gemperli07</a>].   
<p>
NDH-1 produces reactive oxygen species, mainly in the form of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, at the NADH dehydrogenase active site, involving the FMN cofactor [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18307315">Esterhazy08</a>]. NADH-dependent production of hydrogen peroxide is increased in a NuoF E95Q mutant [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24325249">Knuuti13</a>]. The rate of O<sub>2</sub> reduction is dependent on the NAD<sup>+</sup>/NADH ratio [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18307315">Esterhazy08</a>]. 
<p>
Purified NDH-1 is activated by detergent and phospholipids [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15938640">Sinegina05</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14970214">Stolpe04</a>]. A tightly bound metal, most likely Ca<sup>2+</sup>, is required for activity [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20840839">Verkhovskaya11</a>] and stability [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29668960">Belevich18</a>]. Proteins involved in the assembly and stability of NDH-1 have been identified [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30251413">Burschel19</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32777304">Oppermann20</a>]. Exposure to tellurite damages NDH-1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25447814">DiazVasquez15</a>].
<p>
Mutants lacking NDH-1 can not compete with wild type in stationary phase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8366049">Zambrano93</a>]. Expression of the <i>nuo</i> operon is regulated by oxygen, nitrate, fumarate, and other factors including C4 dicarboxylates [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7565112">Bongaerts95</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9063459">Tran97</a>]. Transcription and activity of aerobic respiratory chain components in the different phases of aerobic growth have been measured [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22700653">Sousa12</a>].
<p>
A phylogenomics analysis of NDH-1 subunits suggested that an ancestral NDH-1 complex may have already been present in the Last Universal Cellular Ancestor (LUCA) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27449624">Novakovsky16</a>].
<p>
Mutations in NDH-1 components, predominantly in the membrane arm of the complex, were identified in a laboratory evolution experiment selecting for increased persister cell formation upon entry into stationary phase. The mutations generally impair the proton translocation activity of NDH-1; the resulting cytoplasmic acidification appears to be the cause for increased persister cell formation [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/35087069">Van22</a>].
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26944855">Gnandt16</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26807915">Berrisford16</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26682761">Friedrich16</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24973951">Sato14</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25077450">NakamaruOgiso14</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24059518">Sazanov13</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23701194">Kanjee13</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20505714">Ohnishi10</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18394423">Schneider08a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17274631">Sazanov07</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14741580">Friedrich04</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12600193">Yagi03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11695826">Friedrich01a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10940377">Friedrich00a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9593887">Ohnishi98</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9593861">Friedrich98a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7984099">Neijssel94</a>, <a href="http://www.ecosal.org/">EcoSal</a>]

<comment datatype="string"><i>narGHI</i> encodes a membrane bound quinol-nitrate oxidoreductase, known as nitrate reductase A (NRA) in <i>E. coli</i> K-12. Nitrate reductase A is a respiratory enzyme that functions as a terminal reductase in electron transport pathways that operate during anaerobic growth in the presence of nitrate (see reviews by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8534676">Berks95</a>] and [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>]). 
<p>
The NRA heterotrimer consists of a molybdenum cofactor containing &alpha; subunit (NarG), an Fe-S cluster containing &beta; subunit (NarH) and a heme containing &gamma; subunit (NarI) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4137146">MacGregor74</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4151408">Forget74</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/782444">Clegg76</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1099093">Enoch75</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3053688">Sodergren88a</a>]. The redox active prosthetic groups of NRA form an electron transport chain which uses electrons from the membrane quinone pool for the reduction of cytoplasmic nitrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8899720">vanderOost96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12910261">Bertero03</a>]. Electrons derived from the oxidation of quinol are transferred through two hemes in NarI, one [3Fe-4S] (known as FS4) and three [4Fe-4S] clusters (FS3, FS2 and FS1) in NarH and one [4Fe-4S] (FS0) cluster in NarG to the Mos-bisPGD (molybdo-<i>bis</i>(pyranopterin guanine dinucleotide)) cofactor where nitrate is reduced to nitrite [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10504245">Rothery99a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12731882">Zhao03c</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11321583">Rothery01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15122898">Rothery04</a>] 
<p>
Nitrate reductase A can use both ubiquinol and menaquinol as electron donors [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2204318">Wissenbach90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1444716">Wissenbach92</a>]. Kinetic studies suggest that menadiol and duroquinol (analogues of menaquinone and ubiquinone respectively) react at different sites on NRA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9428711">Giordani97</a>]. Nitrate reductase A has a  H+/e<sup>-</sup> ratio of 1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>].  
<p>
A crystal structure of the catalytic and electron transfer subunits (NarG and NarH) has been solved at 2.0 &Aring;
resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14725769">Jormakka04</a>], and structures of the NarGHI complex both alone and in complex with the quinol binding site (Q-site) inhibitor pentachlorophenol have been solved at 1.9 and 2 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12910261">Bertero03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15615728">Bertero05</a>]. NarGH is localised on the cytosolic side of the inner membrane and interacts with the membrane bound NarI subunit through a hydrophobic interface. Eight redox centres form an arc through the centre of the heterotrimer and are suggestive of a pathway for electron transfer from menaquinol to the nitrate reducing site in NarG. NarGHI forms a homodimer <i>in vitro</i> and probably <i>in vivo</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12910261">Bertero03</a>].  
<p>
 A fourth polypeptide encoded by the <i>narJ</i> gene, is required for the incorporation of the molybdenum cofactor into NarG, the &alpha; subunit [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1732220">Dubourdieu92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1545706">Blasco92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9632249">Blasco98</a>]. If it is coexpressed with the private chaperone NarJ, the NarGH complex alone is soluble and active with artificial electron donors such as benzyl viologen.  NarGH becomes localized to the cytoplasmic side of the inner membrane by interaction with NarI [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1545706">Blasco92</a>].
<p>
Nitrate reductase is responsible for the tellurite reductase activity associated with <i>E. coli</i> membranes. An <i>E. coli</i> strain lacking the membrane associated nitrate reductases is hypersensitive to tellurite under aerobic conditions. A mutant strain which synthesizes nitrate reductase A in large quantities can grow anaereobically with tellurite as the sole electron acceptor. It is not clear whether nitrate reductase is responsible for the total reduction of tellurite to elemental tellurium or whether this reaction is the result of two steps [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9141681">Avazeri97</a>].
<p>
<i>narGHJ</i> and <i>I</i> form an operon in <i>E. coli</i> K-12 which is induced upon anaerobic growth in the presence of nitrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2832376">Sodergren88</a>]. <i>narGHJI</i> is weakly expressed when nitrate levels are low and maximally expressed when nitrate levels are high [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464201">Wang99e</a>]
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 contains three nitrate reductases.  Two of them, nitrate reductase A (NRA) and <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NITRATREDUCTZ-CPLX">nitrate reductase Z</a> (NRZ), are membrane bound and biochemically similar (reviewed in [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7747940">Bonnefoy94</a>]. The third nitrate reductase, <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NAP-CPLX">Nap</a>, is located in the periplasm [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8830238">Grove96</a>].  
<p>
<i>nar</i>: <U>n</U>itr<U>a</U>te <U>r</U>eductase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7047497">Stewart82</a>]
<p>

<comment datatype="string"><i>narGHI</i> encodes a membrane bound quinol-nitrate oxidoreductase, known as nitrate reductase A (NRA) in <i>E. coli</i> K-12. Nitrate reductase A is a respiratory enzyme that functions as a terminal reductase in electron transport pathways that operate during anaerobic growth in the presence of nitrate (see reviews by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8534676">Berks95</a>] and [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>]). 
<p>
The NRA heterotrimer consists of a molybdenum cofactor containing &alpha; subunit (NarG), an Fe-S cluster containing &beta; subunit (NarH) and a heme containing &gamma; subunit (NarI) [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4137146">MacGregor74</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4151408">Forget74</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/782444">Clegg76</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1099093">Enoch75</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3053688">Sodergren88a</a>]. The redox active prosthetic groups of NRA form an electron transport chain which uses electrons from the membrane quinone pool for the reduction of cytoplasmic nitrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8899720">vanderOost96</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12910261">Bertero03</a>]. Electrons derived from the oxidation of quinol are transferred through two hemes in NarI, one [3Fe-4S] (known as FS4) and three [4Fe-4S] clusters (FS3, FS2 and FS1) in NarH and one [4Fe-4S] (FS0) cluster in NarG to the Mos-bisPGD (molybdo-<i>bis</i>(pyranopterin guanine dinucleotide)) cofactor where nitrate is reduced to nitrite [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10504245">Rothery99a</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12731882">Zhao03c</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11321583">Rothery01</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15122898">Rothery04</a>] 
<p>
Nitrate reductase A can use both ubiquinol and menaquinol as electron donors [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2204318">Wissenbach90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1444716">Wissenbach92</a>]. Kinetic studies suggest that menadiol and duroquinol (analogues of menaquinone and ubiquinone respectively) react at different sites on NRA [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9428711">Giordani97</a>]. Nitrate reductase A has a  H+/e<sup>-</sup> ratio of 1 [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9230919">Unden97</a>].  
<p>
A crystal structure of the catalytic and electron transfer subunits (NarG and NarH) has been solved at 2.0 &Aring;
resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14725769">Jormakka04</a>], and structures of the NarGHI complex both alone and in complex with the quinol binding site (Q-site) inhibitor pentachlorophenol have been solved at 1.9 and 2 &Aring; resolution [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12910261">Bertero03</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15615728">Bertero05</a>]. NarGH is localised on the cytosolic side of the inner membrane and interacts with the membrane bound NarI subunit through a hydrophobic interface. Eight redox centres form an arc through the centre of the heterotrimer and are suggestive of a pathway for electron transfer from menaquinol to the nitrate reducing site in NarG. NarGHI forms a homodimer <i>in vitro</i> and probably <i>in vivo</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12910261">Bertero03</a>].  
<p>
 A fourth polypeptide encoded by the <i>narJ</i> gene, is required for the incorporation of the molybdenum cofactor into NarG, the &alpha; subunit [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1732220">Dubourdieu92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1545706">Blasco92</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9632249">Blasco98</a>]. If it is coexpressed with the private chaperone NarJ, the NarGH complex alone is soluble and active with artificial electron donors such as benzyl viologen.  NarGH becomes localized to the cytoplasmic side of the inner membrane by interaction with NarI [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1545706">Blasco92</a>].
<p>
Nitrate reductase is responsible for the tellurite reductase activity associated with <i>E. coli</i> membranes. An <i>E. coli</i> strain lacking the membrane associated nitrate reductases is hypersensitive to tellurite under aerobic conditions. A mutant strain which synthesizes nitrate reductase A in large quantities can grow anaereobically with tellurite as the sole electron acceptor. It is not clear whether nitrate reductase is responsible for the total reduction of tellurite to elemental tellurium or whether this reaction is the result of two steps [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9141681">Avazeri97</a>].
<p>
<i>narGHJ</i> and <i>I</i> form an operon in <i>E. coli</i> K-12 which is induced upon anaerobic growth in the presence of nitrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2832376">Sodergren88</a>]. <i>narGHJI</i> is weakly expressed when nitrate levels are low and maximally expressed when nitrate levels are high [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10464201">Wang99e</a>]
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 contains three nitrate reductases.  Two of them, nitrate reductase A (NRA) and <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NITRATREDUCTZ-CPLX">nitrate reductase Z</a> (NRZ), are membrane bound and biochemically similar (reviewed in [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7747940">Bonnefoy94</a>]. The third nitrate reductase, <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NAP-CPLX">Nap</a>, is located in the periplasm [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8830238">Grove96</a>].  
<p>
<i>nar</i>: <U>n</U>itr<U>a</U>te <U>r</U>eductase [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7047497">Stewart82</a>]
<p>
Reviews: [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11289300">Blasco01</a>]

<comment datatype="string">Nitrate reductase Z (NRZ) is a membrane bound molybdoenzyme responsible for the weak nitrate reductase activity present when cells are grown aerobically in a nitrate containing medium [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3311749">Iobbi87</a>].  
<p>

By homology whith nitrate reductase A, nitrate reductase Z is a heterotrimer composed of the &alpha; (NarZ), &beta; (NarY) and &gamma; (NarV) chains.  A fourth polypeptide, encoded by <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=EG10645"><i>narW</i></a>, is required for the incorporation of the molybdenum cofactor into the &alpha; subunit [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2233673">Blasco90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1545706">Blasco92</a>].
<p>
NRZ is constitutively expressed in a strain which carries the operon on a multicopy plasmid [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3311749">Iobbi87</a>]; NRZ is repressed by Fnr in anaerobiosis; NRZ is only slightly induced by nitrate; NRZ may function during the aerobic to anaerobic transition when cells are growing in the presence of nitrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2139607">IobbiNivol90</a>]. During entry into stationary phase, transcription of the <i>narZYWV</i> operon is induced, and induction is mainly dependent on the alternative sigma factor RpoS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10564515">Chang99c</a>]. 
<p>
Nitrate reductase Z also has tellurite reductase activity in wild-type <i>E. coli</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9141681">Avazeri97</a>].
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 contains three nitrate reductases. Two of them, <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NITRATREDUCTA-CPLX">nitrate reductase A</a> (NRA) and nitrate reductase Z (NRZ), are membrane bound and biochemically similar but differentially regulated (reviewed by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7747940">Bonnefoy94</a>].  The third nitrate reductase, <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NAP-CPLX">Nap</a> is located in the periplasm.
</comment>

<comment datatype="string">Nitrate reductase Z (NRZ) is a membrane bound molybdoenzyme responsible for the weak nitrate reductase activity present when cells are grown aerobically in a nitrate containing medium [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3311749">Iobbi87</a>].  
<p>

By homology whith nitrate reductase A, nitrate reductase Z is a heterotrimer composed of the &alpha; (NarZ), &beta; (NarY) and &gamma; (NarV) chains.  A fourth polypeptide, encoded by <a href="/gene?orgid=ECOLI&id=EG10645"><i>narW</i></a>, is required for the incorporation of the molybdenum cofactor into the &alpha; subunit [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2233673">Blasco90</a>, <a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1545706">Blasco92</a>].
<p>
NRZ is constitutively expressed in a strain which carries the operon on a multicopy plasmid [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3311749">Iobbi87</a>]; NRZ is repressed by Fnr in anaerobiosis; NRZ is only slightly induced by nitrate; NRZ may function during the aerobic to anaerobic transition when cells are growing in the presence of nitrate [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2139607">IobbiNivol90</a>]. During entry into stationary phase, transcription of the <i>narZYWV</i> operon is induced, and induction is mainly dependent on the alternative sigma factor RpoS [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10564515">Chang99c</a>]. 
<p>
Nitrate reductase Z also has tellurite reductase activity in wild-type <i>E. coli</i> [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9141681">Avazeri97</a>].
<p>
<i>E. coli</i> K-12 contains three nitrate reductases. Two of them, <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NITRATREDUCTA-CPLX">nitrate reductase A</a> (NRA) and nitrate reductase Z (NRZ), are membrane bound and biochemically similar but differentially regulated (reviewed by [<a href="http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7747940">Bonnefoy94</a>].  The third nitrate reductase, <a href="/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=ENZYME&object=NAP-CPLX">Nap</a> is located in the periplasm.
</comment>
